title: Harmeet Dhillon Resigns as Justice Department Civil Rights Chief After Midterms
excerpt: The India-born assistant attorney general is the first senior Trump official to leave since Democrats took the House and Senate. She says she was not asked to resign; CBS sources give a different account.
body:
• Harmeet Dhillon resigned on Thursday, November 5, as assistant attorney general for civil rights, after 18 months leading the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division.
  • She is the first senior Trump administration official to leave since Tuesday's midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of the House and Senate.
  • Dhillon told Fox News she was not asked to resign and had told White House chief of staff Susie Wiles in early October that she planned to leave after the midterms; CBS News sources said President Trump had demanded she be fired after her October 18 "60 Minutes" appearance.
  • Her successor must be appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate — now under Democratic control.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general who led the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, resigned on Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced. "Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," Blanche wrote in a post on X, according to CNN. "Serving my country as AAG for Civil Rights has been the honor of a lifetime," Dhillon said in a statement reported by the New York Post.

Two accounts of why she left

Dhillon told Fox News that the decision was hers and came weeks before the election. "I wasn't asked to resign," she said, according to American Kahani's account of her interviews. She said she told Wiles about three weeks before Election Day that she had accomplished what she came to do and wanted to return to private practice, and that Wiles asked her to wait until after the midterms. Her last meeting with Wiles before the elections was on October 13, the Post reported, and she formally submitted her resignation to President Trump and Blanche on November 5. Bloomberg, as cited by The Daily Signal, reported she plans to return to her firm, Dhillon Law Group.

"CNN reported that more than 75% of the Civil Rights Division was fired or quit during her term."

CBS News reported a conflicting account: two sources familiar with the matter told CBS that Trump demanded she be fired after watching her October 18 appearance on "60 Minutes" discussing the government's election integrity efforts, and that Justice Department officials stalled so she could proceed with her plan to resign after the election. Both accounts agree on the timing of her stated intention — early October, before the midterms.

An 18-month remaking of the division

The India-born attorney had led the division since April 2025. In her resignation letter, Dhillon cited efforts aimed at "[e]nding unlawful and discriminatory DEI practices at major institutions across the country" and "[p]rotecting women and girls' sports from biological males, including through lawsuits against Minnesota and California," along with defending Second Amendment rights. She investigated schools over race-based admissions, hiring and training after the Supreme Court's 2023 decision ending affirmative action, took charge of the department's election integrity efforts, and oversaw what the division described as the largest election-monitoring effort in its history during the 2026 midterms. She also dropped pending consent decrees with the Minneapolis and Louisville police departments and rescinded misconduct findings against six other departments, CBS News reported.

Critics described the tenure in starkly different terms. CNN reported that more than 75% of the Civil Rights Division was fired or quit during her term. Stacey Young, a former division attorney who founded Justice Connection, called Dhillon "the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history," in comments reported by American Kahani. The NAACP said in a statement on November 5 that Dhillon had "abdicated her responsibility to enforce our nation's federal civil rights laws," in the words of its general counsel, Kristen Clarke.

What happens next

Dhillon's replacement will need to be appointed by President Trump and confirmed by the US Senate, which Democrats now control after the midterms. Unlike Dhillon's own confirmation, a successor will face a Senate majority from the opposing party, in a division whose direction — on university admissions, police oversight, voter-roll lawsuits and women's sports — has been one of the administration's most contested fronts. No successor has been announced.
